summary: Specifies conventions for using FTP and HTTP to obtain certificates and certificate revocation lists from PKI repositories, satisfying some of the operational requirements of the Internet PKI.

eli5.summary: This explains how to download digital ID cards and the lists of cancelled ones using ordinary web and file-transfer tools.

questions: fetch certificates over http or ftp
how to fetch a certificate over http
subtitle: How to publish and fetch X.509 certificates and revocation lists with plain FTP and HTTP.

tldr.problem: Certificates and CRLs are normally distributed through the Directory, but Directory services are not available in many parts of the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: Put each certificate or CRL in a file with a .cer or .crl suffix, DER encoded, reachable by an ftp or http URI, and register two MIME types, application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl.
tldr.outcome: Anyone who has a URI can fetch a certificate or CRL with tools that are widely deployed and accepted by many firewalls. It does not help find a certificate for a person you only know by e-mail address.

today: RFC 2585 is a Proposed Standard published in May 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where This Fits in the Internet PKI
sections.content:
RFC 2585 is one part of a multi-part standard for the Internet Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) built on X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). It specifies conventions for using FTP and HTTP to obtain certificates and CRLs from PKI repositories. Other mechanisms for repository access are specified in separate documents.

The RFC describes a simplified model with these components: the end entity (a certificate user or the subject of a certificate), the CA (certification authority), the optional RA (registration authority, to which a CA delegates some management functions) and the repository, a system or set of systems that stores certificates and CRLs and distributes them to end entities.
sections.eli5: There is a system for handing out digital ID cards. This note covers one small job in it: how to get hold of the cards and the cancelled-card lists.

sections.title: Why Use FTP and HTTP
sections.content:
Some CAs require online validation services, while others distribute CRLs so certificate users can validate certificates themselves. CRLs and certificates are generally published in the Directory. The RFC notes, however, that Directory services are not available in many parts of the Internet today, so FTP (RFC 959) and HTTP (RFC 2068) are offered as alternatives.

End entities and CAs may retrieve certificates and CRLs from the repository with FTP or HTTP. End entities may publish their own certificate, and RAs and CAs may publish certificates and CRLs, the same way.
sections.eli5: The usual place to find these cards is not reachable from everywhere. Ordinary file and web servers are, so they make a good backup place.

sections.title: FTP and HTTP Conventions
sections.content:
Certificate and CRL extensions can carry a URI in the GeneralName form to say where issuer certificates and CRLs may be obtained. An IA5String describes the use of anonymous FTP or of HTTP. The examples are ftp://ftp.your.org/pki/id48.cer and http://www.your.org/pki/id48.no42.crl.

File names should carry a suffix: .cer for certificates and .crl for CRLs. Each .cer file holds exactly one certificate and each .crl file exactly one CRL, both in DER format.

The RFC says people may print the URI of their certificate file on a business card, which helps when there is no Directory entry for them. FTP and HTTP are widely deployed and accommodated by many firewalls. The service only retrieves information tied to a certificate already identified by a URI. It is not meant to find a certificate for a user known only by other details such as an e-mail address or corporate affiliation.
sections.eli5: Each card or list sits in its own file, named ending in .cer or .crl. If you know the web address of the file, you can just download it.

sections.title: The Two MIME Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers two MIME media types so certificates and CRLs can be transferred with the right label: application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl. Each registration has an optional parameter version with a default of 1, and no required parameters.

The encoding is none for 8-bit transports and most likely Base64 for SMTP or other 7-bit transports. The file extensions are .CER and .CRL, and the intended usage is COMMON. The security note for each says it carries a cryptographic certificate or a cryptographic certificate revocation list.
sections.eli5: Each file gets a label saying whether it is a card or a cancelled-cards list, so a program knows what to do when it arrives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Certificates and CRLs are digitally signed, so no extra integrity service is needed. They need not be kept secret and anonymous access is generally acceptable, so no privacy service is needed either.

HTTP caching proxies are common, and some do not check for the latest version of an object correctly. A request for a certificate or CRL through a misconfigured or broken proxy may return an out-of-date response. Operators of FTP sites and web servers should authenticate end entities who publish certificates, and CAs and RAs who publish certificates and CRLs, but authentication is not necessary to retrieve them.
sections.eli5: The cards are signed, so nobody can change them without it showing. Anyone may look at them. The thing to watch is a lazy middleman who hands you an old copy of the list.

items.label: application/pkix-cert
items.desc: One certificate per file, DER encoded.

items.label: application/pkix-crl
items.desc: One CRL per file, DER encoded.
